Homogeneity acceleration is an image-order volume rendering technique that extends empty-space skipping by approximating the contribution of uniform, non-empty regions instead of sampling them voxel-by-voxel [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that homogeneity acceleration is an image-order volume rendering technique that extends empty-space skipping by approximating the contribution of uniform, non-empty regions instead of sampling them voxel-by-voxel. The evidence from both S1 and S2 confirms that Denskin and Hanrahan improved upon presence acceleration (which skips empty segments) by using a range pyramid to approximate homogeneous regions. Specifically, S1 states they used pyramids 'not only for skipping the empty ray segments but for approximate evaluation of homogeneous regions,' and S2 notes this involves 'approximate evaluation of homogeneous regions by using a range pyramid instead of a binary pyramid.' The mechanism described in the claim (approximating uniform regions rather than detailed sampling) aligns with the evidence's description of performing an 'approximate evaluation' when max/min values are nearly the same.

This aligns perfectly with the claim's description of handling regions that contain data (non-empty) but lack internal variation (homogeneous) to reduce computational load.
